turns.reply: Welcome! Pumping up a bike tyre or squeezing a balloon shows gas pressure at work, and it all comes down to tiny gas molecules moving constantly and randomly inside their container. What do you think those molecules do when they reach the container's walls?

turns.student: ugh my phone battery's dying already lol
turns.reply: Ha, fair enough, we'll keep it quick! Here's the idea another way: inside a tyre, billions of tiny gas molecules keep hitting the inner wall, and each hit gives the wall a tiny push. Those pushes all add up to gas pressure. What do the molecules do to the wall every time they hit it?

Every time a molecule hits the wall, it gives the wall a tiny push. Each hit is called a collision, and each collision adds a tiny force to the total pressure. Why does a tyre have a steady pressure, even though each push is so tiny?

No worries, let's make it simpler. Imagine a ball bouncing off a wall: that bounce is a collision, and it gives the wall a tiny push. In a tyre, billions of molecules do this every second. What does each collision give the wall?
Not quite, but you're getting there. Would you like me to just tell you the rest of this one?

turns.student: nah i get it now. they push it right?
turns.reply: Yes — they push it. Each collision is one molecule striking the wall, and it gives the wall a tiny force; with huge numbers of collisions every second, those tiny forces add up to a steady pressure. So what does each collision give the wall?

Yes — each collision gives the wall a tiny force, and loads of them add up to pressure. Next, the temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules, so a hotter gas has faster-moving molecules. If you heat a gas, what happens to the speed of its molecules?
recap: Gas molecules move randomly and constantly, hitting the walls of their container.
Each collision gives the wall a tiny push, which is a tiny force.
Billions of collisions every second add up to a steady pressure.
Pressure is just loads of tiny forces from molecules pushing on the walls.

turns.reply: Let me say that more simply: when you heat a gas, its molecules gain energy and zoom around faster. So a hotter gas just means faster molecules. If you heat a gas, how does the speed of its molecules change?

Yes — hotter gas means faster molecules. Now put that gas in a sealed rigid container, so its volume stays the same, and heat it. The faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often. What happens to the pressure?

Yes — faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure goes up. Now keep the temperature the same and squeeze a fixed mass of gas into half the volume. The pressure and volume multiply to give the same number every time, so p₁V₁ = p₂V₂. If the volume halves, what happens to the pressure?
recap: Pressure comes from loads of tiny molecule collisions pushing on the container walls.
Heating a gas gives its molecules more energy, so they move faster.
In a sealed rigid container, the volume stays the same when you heat the gas.
Faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure rises.

turns.reply: Fair enough, shorter: squeeze a gas into half the space and its molecules hit the walls twice as often, so the pressure doubles. Pressure × volume always stays the same. If the volume halves, what happens to the pressure?

That's fine, the answer is that the pressure doubles. Pressure and volume are inversely proportional, which means when one doubles, the other halves. So if you double the volume of a gas at constant temperature, what happens to the pressure?
No worries. Picture a gas spreading into a space twice as big: its molecules hit the walls less often, so the pressure halves. Now flip it: if you halve the pressure, what happens to the volume?
Do you want me to just tell you the rest of this one?

Let's keep going. Inversely proportional means that when one quantity doubles, the other halves, so pressure × volume always stays the same. So if a gas is squashed into half the space, what happens to its pressure?
Next idea: when you push a piston into a gas, you apply a force to it, and that transfers energy to the gas. So when you push a bike pump handle in, what is being transferred to the air inside?
recap: Squash a gas into half the space and the pressure doubles.
Pressure and volume are inversely proportional: one goes up, the other goes down.
Pressure × volume stays the same, so p₁V₁ = p₂V₂.
Give a gas double the room and its pressure halves.

turns.reply: Yes — energy is right. So when the pump does work on the air, what happens to the air's internal energy?
Yes — the air's internal energy goes up, because the pump transfers energy to it. That brings us to the end of this lesson.
recap: Pushing a piston into a gas applies a force to it.
That force does work, transferring energy to the gas.
The gas's internal energy goes up when work is done on it.
So pushing a bike pump handle in gives the air more energy.

turns.reply: You're welcome! You worked well today, especially on how adding energy to a gas raises its internal energy. Come back any time to go over the rest.
